 The last Friday the 13th of 2026: Mysteries and Interesting Facts
 VHO - November 13, 2026 falls on a Friday, marking the third time this supposedly unlucky day of the year has appeared. Why do so many people fear Friday the 13th?
 Báo Văn Hóa • 12/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 When Friday the 13th is mentioned, many people immediately think of bad luck, superstitions, or famous horror movies. However, not everyone knows the true origin of this belief, nor the fact that there can be up to three Friday the 13ths in a year. 
 Illustration How many Friday the 13ths are there in 2026?
 According to the Gregorian calendar, 2026 will have a total of three Friday the 13ths, falling on February 13th, March 13th, and November 13th, 2026. This is also the maximum number of times Friday the 13th can occur in a year.
 Specifically, November 13, 2026, is the last Friday the 13th of the year. After this date, a similar phenomenon will not occur again until August 13, 2027.
 Interestingly, Friday the 13th doesn't occur with the same frequency every year. Some years it happens only once, some twice, and some years it happens three times, like in 2026. For example, 2025 will only have one Friday the 13th in June, while 2024 will have two in September and December.
 This difference is entirely in accordance with the rules of the calendar and has nothing to do with spiritual factors. In the Gregorian calendar, which is widely used today, any month that begins on a Sunday will have its 13th day fall on a Friday.
 In 2026, February, March, and November will all begin on a Sunday, creating three occurrences of this special day.
 Why is Friday the 13th considered an unlucky day?
 The belief that Friday the 13th brings bad luck primarily originates from Western culture. However, historians and folklorists have yet to identify a single event that marks the birth of this belief.
 You may also like One of the most common explanations relates to Christianity. According to religious tradition, the Last Supper before Jesus' crucifixion had 13 attendees, including Jesus and 12 apostles. Among them was Judas, who is mentioned for betraying Jesus.
 Meanwhile, the day Jesus was crucified is commemorated on Good Friday. The combination of the number 13 and Friday is believed to be one of the factors contributing to the perception of it as an unlucky day.
 Furthermore, the number 13 has long been considered unlucky by some Westerners. This stems partly from the fact that the number 12 is often associated with completeness, such as the 12 months of the year, the 12 zodiac signs, or the 12 hours on a clock. The number 13, appearing shortly after, is therefore sometimes perceived as disrupting this familiar order.
 Another theory links Friday the 13th to the event of October 13, 1307, when King Philip IV of France ordered the mass arrest of Knights Templar. However, even if this historical event is real, there is no reliable evidence to suggest that it directly gave rise to the notion that Friday the 13th is an unlucky day.
 Notably, accounts of the bad luck associated with Friday the 13th have appeared in French literature since the 19th century. By 1907, the novel Friday, the Thirteenth by American writer Thomas W. Lawson further contributed to bringing this concept closer to the public.
 Later, the Friday the 13th horror film series, which began in 1980, further cemented this day's status as a familiar symbol in popular culture. The image of Friday the 13th, associated with fear, mystery, and terrifying situations, gradually became widespread through film, television, and the internet.
 Is Friday the 13th really that scary?
 Despite being associated with many unfortunate stories, there is currently no reliable scientific evidence to prove that Friday the 13th is more dangerous than other days.
 From a psychological perspective, when people believe a particular day will bring bad luck, they tend to pay more attention to and remember the negative events that occur on that day. Conversely, positive or ordinary things are less likely to be noticed.
 For example, if someone accidentally drops something, is late, or encounters a problem at work on Friday the 13th, they might immediately associate the incident with the supposedly unlucky day. Meanwhile, if the same thing happened on another day, they might simply view it as a coincidence.
 You may also like In fact, perceptions of unlucky days vary across cultures. While Friday the 13th is popular in many Western countries, some Spanish -speaking nations are particularly wary of Tuesday the 13th. In Italy, Friday the 17th is more commonly associated with bad luck.
 In Vietnam, Friday the 13th is not a traditional holiday or taboo day. The concept of this day is primarily known through films, books, and cultural exchange.
 Some people may choose to be more cautious when making important decisions on this day, but there's no scientific reason to postpone work, travel, or pre-planned activities simply because of the calendar.
 Therefore, Friday, November 13, 2026, can be seen as an interesting coincidence in the Gregorian calendar and an opportunity to learn more about history, beliefs, and how people have formed cultural concepts over generations.
 Instead of worrying about bad luck, it's important to maintain a relaxed mindset, act cautiously, and make decisions based on factual information. After all, whether a day is good or not depends on many factors, and cannot be determined solely by the numbers on a calendar.
